passage.title: Mirrors in the Cold Dark
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
Light from the first stars has traveled across space for more than thirteen billion years. As the universe expands, it stretches those ancient light waves until they shift past what human eyes can see. They become faint infrared rays, which we feel on Earth as gentle heat. Because warm air and glowing dust in our own sky block those weak signals, ground telescopes cannot spot them clearly. To capture that ancient starlight, engineers had to send the James Webb Space Telescope far beyond the moon.

The craft orbits at a stable balance spot in deep space called the second Lagrange point, or L2. Here, the pull of Earth and the Sun hold the telescope steady on a cold, dark path. One million miles from Earth, the eighteen gold-coated mirror segments made of light beryllium were unfolded by tiny motors after the sunshield was locked tight. This rare metal stays stiff in deep freeze and weighs far less than glass. A five-layer kite of thin film blocks heat from the Sun and Earth so warmth does not impede the sensors.

In that deep chill, the main mirror works like a giant bucket for catching faint heat drops from young galaxies. Each six-sided plate is polished until its curve is smooth within a fraction of a human hair. Tiny rods behind each plate nudge the metal segments until all eighteen pieces act as one wide eye. Working together, they preserve the crisp shape of distant star clusters that formed soon after cosmic dawn.

Even with a twenty-foot gold mirror, some early stars are still too dim for the telescope to see alone. Fortunately, space itself provides a natural booster through an effect known as gravitational lensing. When a massive cluster of galaxies sits between the telescope and a deeper star, its huge gravity bends the fabric of space. Like a thick glass lens, that curved space acts to magnify the background light into bright arcs and rings.

By aiming the cold mirror at these gravity lenses, scientists can study galaxies that would otherwise stay hidden forever. Sensors on the craft split the stretched light into a rainbow code that reveals subtle traces of oxygen, carbon, and neon. Step by step, human tools at L2 now team up with giant cosmic lenses. Together, they are rewriting the story of how the first stars were born.

monsterSentence.verbatimSentence: One million miles from Earth, the eighteen gold-coated mirror segments made of light beryllium were unfolded by tiny motors after the sunshield was locked tight.
distractorChunks: after the sunshield was locked tight
monsterSentence.activeRewrite: One million miles from Earth, tiny motors unfolded the eighteen gold-coated mirror segments made of light beryllium after locking the sunshield tight.

tier2Words.definition: To block, slow down, or get in the way of a process
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'impedire' meaning to shackle the feet
tier2Words.contextClue: The five-layer sunshield blocks heat from the Sun and Earth so warmth does not interfere with the cold sensors.

tier2Words.definition: To keep something safe, intact, or in its original state
tier2Words.contextClue: Aligning all eighteen mirror pieces keeps the crisp shape of distant star clusters clear.

tier2Words.definition: To make something appear larger, brighter, or stronger
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'magnus' meaning great or large
tier2Words.contextClue: Like a thick glass lens, curved space boosts and enlarges faint background light into bright arcs.

tier2Words.definition: Faint, delicate, or hard to detect without close inspection
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'subtilis' meaning fine or delicately woven
tier2Words.contextClue: Special sensors split the stretched light to spot faint chemical traces of oxygen and carbon.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"One million miles from Earth, the eighteen gold-coated mirror segments made of light beryllium were unfolded by tiny motors after the sunshield was locked tight."

In this sentence, what performed the action of unfolding the mirror segments?

options.text: The light beryllium that formed the eighteen gold-coated segments
options.childFeedback: Light beryllium is the rare metal the mirror segments are made of; a metal material cannot unfold itself without motors.

options.text: The five-layer sunshield that was locked tight
options.childFeedback: The sunshield was locked tight before the mirrors opened ('after the sunshield was locked tight'), while the tiny motors did the unfolding.

options.text: The tiny motors on the spacecraft
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were unfolded by tiny motors' shows that the tiny motors on the spacecraft performed the action of unfolding the eighteen mirror segments.

options.text: The pull of Earth one million miles away
options.childFeedback: Earth's gravity helps hold the telescope on its orbit path at L2, but tiny motors on the craft unfolded the mirror segments.

questions.provingSentenceText: One million miles from Earth, the eighteen gold-coated mirror segments made of light beryllium were unfolded by tiny motors after the sunshield was locked tight.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were unfolded by tiny motors' shows that the tiny motors on the spacecraft performed the action of unfolding the eighteen mirror segments.
questions.parentExplanation: The passive verb 'were unfolded by' is separated from the grammatical subject ('mirror segments') by the participial phrase 'made of light beryllium.' The agent performing the unfolding is 'tiny motors.'
questions.retryHint: Look at the words right after 'unfolded by' in the Paragraph 2 sentence to see what opened the mirror segments.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"A five-layer kite of thin film blocks heat from the Sun and Earth so warmth does not impede the sensors."

What does the word "impede" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: Power or recharge
options.childFeedback: Warmth does not power the infrared sensors—heat would blind them to faint infrared rays from distant stars, which is why the sunshield blocks warmth.

options.text: Interfere with or block
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, 'impede' means to interfere with or block, because the sunshield blocks heat from the Sun and Earth so that warmth does not interfere with the cold infrared sensors.

options.text: Polish or brighten
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that the six-sided plates were already polished smooth before launch; stray heat in space interferes with sensors rather than polishing them.

options.text: Destroy completely forever
options.childFeedback: Warmth from the Sun or Earth would interfere with the sensors' ability to read faint heat signals, not blow up or destroy the spacecraft forever.

questions.provingSentenceText: A five-layer kite of thin film blocks heat from the Sun and Earth so warmth does not impede the sensors.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, 'impede' means to interfere with or block, because the sunshield blocks heat from the Sun and Earth so that warmth does not interfere with the cold infrared sensors.
questions.parentExplanation: Because the telescope detects faint infrared heat signals, stray warmth from the Sun or Earth would interfere with ('impede') the sensors' ability to read distant starlight.
questions.retryHint: Remember from Paragraph 1 and Paragraph 2 that the telescope needs deep cold to detect faint heat rays, and see why the sunshield blocks warmth from reaching the sensors.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 1, why has ancient starlight turned into infrared rays by the time it reaches the telescope?

options.text: Warm air and glowing dust in Earth's sky heat the light waves up as they pass the moon.
options.childFeedback: Warm air and dust in Earth's sky block infrared signals from reaching ground telescopes, but the light shifted into infrared during its thirteen-billion-year journey through expanding space.

options.text: The gold coating on the eighteen mirror segments turns every beam of light into heat.
options.childFeedback: The ancient starlight is already infrared before it ever reaches the telescope's gold-coated mirrors at L2.

options.text: The expanding universe stretches the traveling light waves beyond visible light.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains that as the universe expands over thirteen billion years, it stretches the ancient light waves until they shift beyond visible light into faint infrared rays.

options.text: Ancient stars only ever gave off invisible heat instead of bright light when they formed.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 states that the light waves shifted 'past what human eyes can see' as the universe expanded and stretched them over billions of years.

questions.provingSentenceText: As the universe expands, it stretches those ancient light waves until they shift past what human eyes can see.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 explains that as the universe expands over thirteen billion years, it stretches the ancient light waves until they shift beyond visible light into faint infrared rays.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 explicitly explains the cause-and-effect relationship: as the universe expands over billions of years, it stretches the ancient light waves until they shift past visible light into infrared rays.
questions.retryHint: Read the second and third sentences of Paragraph 1 to see what the expanding universe does to ancient light waves as they travel.

questions.prompt: Why does the author compare curved space to "a thick glass lens" in Paragraph 4?

options.text: To help readers understand how the gravity of a massive galaxy cluster bends and boosts dim starlight behind it
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, the author compares curved space to 'a thick glass lens' to help readers picture how the gravity of a massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies dim starlight behind it.

options.text: To prove that the telescope's mirrors should have been made of thick glass instead of beryllium
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 explains that beryllium is much better than glass for the telescope's mirrors because it stays stiff in deep freeze and weighs far less.

options.text: To show that solid glass clouds float between distant galaxies in deep space
options.childFeedback: There is no actual glass floating between galaxies—'Like a thick glass lens' is a simile comparing curved space to a magnifying glass.

options.text: To explain why tiny rods behind each mirror plate must nudge the segments into a curve
options.childFeedback: Tiny rods nudging the beryllium mirror plates are described in Paragraph 3, whereas the 'thick glass lens' simile in Paragraph 4 describes gravity in deep space.

questions.provingSentenceText: Like a thick glass lens, that curved space acts to magnify the background light into bright arcs and rings.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, the author compares curved space to 'a thick glass lens' to help readers picture how the gravity of a massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies dim starlight behind it.
questions.parentExplanation: The analogy in Paragraph 4 compares space curved by a galaxy cluster's gravity to a thick glass lens because both bend and magnify faint light passing through them.
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 4 to see what 'Like a thick glass lens, that curved space acts to...' explains.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best explains how human engineering and natural cosmic forces work together in the passage?

options.text: The Sun's heat warms the beryllium mirror segments so they can bend gravity around the moon.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 stresses that the five-layer sunshield blocks the Sun's heat to keep the beryllium mirror in a deep freeze, not warm.

options.text: The telescope's cold mirror captures faint infrared rays that have already been magnified by the gravity of galaxy clusters.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 4 and 5 show that massive galaxy clusters act as natural gravity lenses that magnify dim background light, and engineers aim the Webb telescope's cold mirror at those lenses to study hidden galaxies.

options.text: Ground telescopes on Earth bounce laser beams off the five-layer sunshield at the L2 point.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains that ground telescopes are blocked by Earth's warm sky, and the passage never mentions bouncing lasers off the sunshield.

options.text: Gravity lenses completely replace the need for any mirrors or sensors on space telescopes.
options.childFeedback: Scientists still need the twenty-foot gold mirror and onboard sensors at L2 to capture and split the light magnified by gravity lenses.

questions.provingSentenceText: By aiming the cold mirror at these gravity lenses, scientists can study galaxies that would otherwise stay hidden forever.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 4 and 5 show that massive galaxy clusters act as natural gravity lenses that magnify dim background light, and engineers aim the Webb telescope's cold mirror at those lenses to study hidden galaxies.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 4 and 5 show that natural gravitational lensing magnifies distant starlight first, and then scientists aim the chilled Webb mirror at those gravity lenses to capture and analyze the light.
questions.retryHint: Look at the first and third sentences of Paragraph 5 to see how human tools at L2 team up with giant cosmic gravity lenses.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Because warm air and glowing dust in our own sky block those weak signals, ground telescopes cannot spot them clearly."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 only explains why ground telescopes on Earth cannot see faint infrared rays clearly.

options.text: "This rare metal stays stiff in deep freeze and weighs far less than glass."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 2 explains why engineers chose beryllium metal for the mirrors, without mentioning natural cosmic forces like gravity lenses.

options.text: "Each six-sided plate is polished until its curve is smooth within a fraction of a human hair."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 3 describes how smoothly the mirror plates are polished, leaving out how they team up with gravity lenses in deep space.

options.text: "By aiming the cold mirror at these gravity lenses, scientists can study galaxies that would otherwise stay hidden forever."
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by showing how scientists aim the human-built cold mirror at natural cosmic gravity lenses to study distant galaxies.

questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by showing how scientists aim the human-built cold mirror at natural cosmic gravity lenses to study distant galaxies.
